repos.title: Optimizing the Interface Between Knowledge Graphs and LLMs for Complex Reasoning
repos.paper_summary:
Dreamify is a hyperparameter optimization framework for Cognee, a modular system that constructs knowledge graphs and retrieves context for LLMs. It uses Tree-structured Parzen Estimator to tune six parameters: chunk size, retriever type, top-k count, QA prompt, graph extraction prompt, and task preprocessing method. The authors evaluate on filtered subsets of HotPotQA, TwoWikiMultiHop, and MuSiQue, using 24 training and 12 test instances per dataset. Each experiment runs 50 trials, scoring configurations by exact match, F1, or DeepEval correctness.

Optimization yields consistent gains over default baselines. For example, HotPotQA exact match rises from 0.042 to 0.667, and F1 increases from 0.169 to 0.840. On the held-out test sets, performance generally remains above baseline but drops slightly compared to training scores; however, TwoWikiMultiHop F1 improves from 0.625 in training to 0.704 in testing. The paper notes that small evaluation sets introduce variability, and no single configuration performs best across all benchmarks, indicating that optimal settings are task-specific.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Hyperparameter tuning of graph-enhanced retrieval pipelines is underexamined, though many interacting settings affect multi-hop question answering.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work covers retrieval-augmented pipelines, three multi-hop benchmarks, graph-based question answering, and prior optimization of such pipelines.

digest_headlines.heading: Automated Knowledge Graph Construction: Cognee
digest_headlines.headline: Cognee is an open-source framework whose modular pipeline and built-in evaluation let the whole system serve as an optimization objective.

digest_headlines.heading: Hyperparameter Optimization Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Dreamify tunes six Cognee parameters with a Tree-structured Parzen Estimator, scoring each trial by a benchmark metric averaged over questions.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Setup
digest_headlines.headline: Nine experiments pair three datasets with three metrics, each running 50 trials on 24 training and 12 test instances per dataset.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Tuned settings beat baselines on all nine training metrics, but most hold-out scores fell below training scores.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Tuning gave consistent but uneven gains, and the authors call for custom benchmarks and better evaluation of graph-based systems.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: Appendix describes Cognee's extract-cognify-load architecture, its default pipeline stages, retriever types, and the evaluation framework.

repos.title: FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
repos.paper_summary: FlexGlue is a neural matcher that takes a set of query keypoints in one image and predicts their subpixel correspondences in the second image, while also predicting whether the pair is covisible so that non-overlapping pairs are rejected. A CNN backbone (frozen ConvNeXt-B with DINOv3 weights) produces a coarse token grid for each image. A 9-layer Transformer with self- and cross-attention updates the tokens, and a per-layer covisibility head can stop inference early on non-overlapping pairs. Each query gets a coarse position from a windowed softmax over cosine similarities, then a learned sub-cell offset. The model is trained on eight datasets with a joint correspondence, matchability, and covisibility loss. The paper reports that FlexGlue performs similarly to LoMa on sparse relative pose, is competitive with RoMav2 at lower cost, and gets the highest HardMatch mAA@10px in the sparse-to-dense setting. It also reports gains on ETH3D and IMC2025 SfM, InLoc, and a new indoor doppelganger benchmark built from LaMAR. Limitations include zero-shot evaluation on indoor disambiguation, since no indoor training data exists, and the paper notes that dense matching lacks robustness on HardMatch.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sparse matchers are fast but detector-bound, dense matchers are costly, and both miss visual symmetries.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior matchers either inherit keypoint detector limits or add separate post-hoc disambiguation models; FlexGlue handles both in one network.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: FlexGlue aggregates context over dense token grids and reads out subpixel correspondences only at query keypoints, with covisibility heads.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Experiments show FlexGlue is competitive with dense matchers on relative pose at lower matching time, and it improves disambiguation, especially indoors.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion claims top accuracy on two multi-view reconstruction benchmarks and on disambiguation and localization benchmarks, at competitive cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists inference cost, keypoint detector results, benchmark curation, training details, matching modes, and limitations such as correlated errors and depth-edge accuracy drops.

repos.title: Spatial Metaphors for LLM Memory: A Critical Analysis of the MemPalace Architecture
repos.paper_summary: This preprint analyzes MemPalace, an open-source memory system for LLMs that organizes stored text as Wings, Rooms, and Drawers. It maps each layer to the code and attributes the reported LongMemEval results to individual components. The authors find that the palace hierarchy is a flat ChromaDB collection with metadata filtering. The 96.6% Recall@5 (at least one correct session in the top five) comes from verbatim text embedded with ChromaDB's default all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model, without palace structure. Room-based boosting reaches 89.4%, and the lossy AAAK mode reaches 84.2%. Mem0's April 2026 algorithm reports 93.4%. The paper credits the verbatim-first design, the zero-LLM write path, and a wake-up cost of about 170 tokens. It finds no computational benefit from the spatial metaphor and no implemented contradiction detection. Limitations: the core analysis covers v3.1.0, later releases are discussed separately, benchmark findings rely partly on a third-party audit and maintainer corrections, and the paper is not peer-reviewed.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Persistent memory for language models is an open problem, and MemPalace's claimed 96.6% Recall@5 prompted this audit.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: The spatial metaphor may help users, the authors argue, but it does not change the underlying vector retrieval.

digest_headlines.heading: System Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: MemPalace's hierarchy is metadata on one flat ChromaDB collection, so wings and rooms act as search filters.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation and Benchmarks
digest_headlines.headline: An independent audit found the 96.6% result reproduces with plain ChromaDB, and six benchmark claims were corrected.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Verbatim storage, zero-LLM writes and low wake-up cost are the main contributions, while metadata filtering and chunking are standard practice.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Systems in Detail
digest_headlines.headline: Every listed competitor calls an LLM at write time, and reported LongMemEval scores vary widely.

digest_headlines.heading: A Framework for Evaluating AI Memory Systems
digest_headlines.headline: A multi-dimensional framework shows MemPalace leads on fidelity, cost and privacy but trails on relational depth and scalability.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: MemPalace is architecturally standard, the authors conclude, yet its verbatim-first insight and zero-cost writes are useful.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists codebase statistics, reproduction conditions, a glossary, and the analysis disclosure for version 3.1.0.

repos.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
repos.paper_summary: SpecPilot is an autonomous agentic loop that searches for lossless speculative decoding optimizations tailored to each deployment. A cost model ranks the largest gaps between the current system and an estimated speedup ceiling, parallel agents explore directions on separate GPUs, and a controller promotes only changes with a significant gain on unseen requests. Token forcing checks every output token against the stock engine, catching lossy changes that task accuracy misses. Validated mechanisms are stored in structured memory and reused across rounds and deployments. Discovered mechanisms include W12, a lossless 12-bit weight format averaging 12.01–12.02 bits per weight; best-first tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets; two-level verification using an 8-bit view of W12 as a low-precision pre-check; and three batching mechanisms. Across four target models, three drafters, two GPUs and five benchmarks, speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding rises from stock's 4.46× to 10.87× with one request, and from 1.94× to 3.93× with batching. On H100 with one request, the paper reports 1.84× faster than DDTree. The gains are reported without training or quality loss. Limitations: the loop depends on agent-driven search, and results are measured only on the listed models, drafters, GPUs and benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Stock parallel-drafter systems leave speedup unrealized, which motivates SpecPilot's per-deployment search.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Lossless speculative decoding accepts only tokens matching the exact target's argmax, so output tests cannot easily verify it.

digest_headlines.heading: SpecPilot
digest_headlines.headline: A cost model finds the largest gap to a ceiling, and a controller accepts changes only on confirmed gains.

digest_headlines.heading: Discovered Lossless Algorithms
digest_headlines.headline: SpecPilot discovered a lossless 12-bit weight format, best-first tree verification, two-level verification and batching mechanisms.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Sealed finals on unseen requests give single-request gains of 2.13× to 2.44× and batching gains of 1.85× to 3.11×.

repos.title: Deep Photo Style Transfer
repos.paper_summary: The paper introduces a deep-learning method for photographic style transfer that preserves the photorealism of the input image while accurately matching the color and texture of a reference style image. The approach extends the Neural Style algorithm by adding two constraints to the optimization objective. First, a photorealism regularization term ensures the transformation from input to output is locally affine in color space, preventing spatial distortions like wiggly edges. This term uses the Matting Laplacian matrix derived from the input image. Second, an augmented style loss incorporates semantic segmentation masks for both images, restricting style transfer between semantically equivalent regions (e.g., sky to sky) to prevent "spillover" artifacts. The method uses a pre-trained VGG-19 network, with content features from `conv4_2` and style features from layers `conv1_1` through `conv5_1`. Optimization runs in 3–5 minutes on an NVIDIA Titan X GPU. In user studies, the method produced photorealistic results comparable to global histogram transfer methods, but achieved higher style faithfulness than Reinhard et al., Pitié et al., and Photoshop Match Color in over 80% of comparisons. Limitations include failure cases under extreme semantic mismatch between input and reference, which require manual segmentation masks to resolve.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Photographic style transfer must avoid painting-like distortion while keeping the reference style faithful.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method adds a locally affine color regularizer and semantic segmentation masks to Neural Style optimization.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation Details
digest_headlines.headline: The implementation uses a pretrained convolutional network, two-stage optimization and merged segmentation classes.

digest_headlines.heading: Results and Comparison
digest_headlines.headline: Compared with Neural Style, patch-based and global transfer methods, the approach avoids distortion and was judged most faithful more than 80% of the time.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: The approach transfers reference style faithfully across time of day, weather, season and artistic edits while keeping outputs photorealistic.

repos.title: YANchor-4B: Effective Long-Horizon Reasoning in O(N) Time with O(1) Memory
repos.paper_summary: EdgeRock is a family of multimodal reasoning models whose persistent history stays fixed in size however long the model reasons. Its first release, EdgeRock-4B, is converted from Qwen3.5-4B and adds Rock Memory Anchors (RMA). A learned writer produces a key-value record for each token, and a learned scorer rates it. Every 256 tokens, each of four KV groups keeps its 1,024 highest-scoring records from the committed bank and the new candidates. Queries read these records directly, alongside a 1,024-token sliding window and gated DeltaNet recurrent state. Attention KV is 72 MiB per sequence, versus 8 GiB for a 256K-token full-attention cache. On AIME 2024–2026, EdgeRock-4B reaches 82.9% mean pass@1, while the 16 bounded-state models evaluated, up to 14B parameters, reach at most 18.8%. Disabling RMA at inference lowers long-context query accuracy from 94.1% to 0.4%. Throughput is up to 6.42× that of Qwen3.5-4B on one 80GB GPU, measured at 32K input and 32K output with repeated prompts. Limitations: only the 4B model is released, and larger sizes are stated as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Growing reasoning caches strain serving and edge budgets, and bounded-state models lose reasoning, so EdgeRock adds learned fixed-size anchors.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 How is EdgeRock built?
digest_headlines.headline: EdgeRock-4B converts Qwen3.5-4B by replacing full attention with a 1,024-position window plus an RMA module in four training stages.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 How does RMA preserve distant information?
digest_headlines.headline: RMA keeps the highest-scoring records in a fixed bank of 1,024 per group, updated every 256 tokens, and any query can read them.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 What stays constant as context grows?
digest_headlines.headline: Persistent history per sequence stays fixed in size however long the model reasons, unlike a full-attention cache that grows with each token.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Evaluation design
digest_headlines.headline: The evaluation compares 28 models on 29 text benchmarks and measures visual reasoning, distant memory, and long-sequence inference.

digest_headlines.heading: 6 Does strong reasoning survive constant memory?
digest_headlines.headline: EdgeRock-4B reaches 82.9% on AIME 2024–2026 and retains 96.3% of its Qwen3.5-4B source's AIME mean.

digest_headlines.heading: 7 Do distant answers depend on RMA?
digest_headlines.headline: Disabling RMA at inference drops query accuracy from 94.1% to 0.4%, showing distant answers flow through the anchor bank.

digest_headlines.heading: 8 What does constant memory buy in deployment?
digest_headlines.headline: EdgeRock-4B runs 512 long-generation sequences at once on one accelerator and averages 4.94 times Qwen3.5-4B's end-to-end throughput.

digest_headlines.heading: 9 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Fixed history makes memory a design-time property, which the authors argue lets robots, chips, and agents plan capacity before reasoning.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the text and visual evaluation protocols, bounded-state and compact benchmark tables, runtime tables, and the state-ownership specification.

repos.title: Skill Training with Corruption and Reconstruction Loop
repos.paper_summary: Skill Training with Corruption and Reconstruction Loop proposes a self-supervised way for LLM agents to learn domain skills as an external text library, without updating model weights, human annotations, or external rewards. Human-written short-drama screenplays are corrupted into story outlines, and the agent reconstructs each script using its skill library. A loss agent compares the reconstruction with the original and produces a textual loss report, and a backward agent edits the relevant skill cards. Skill cards are routed into Mixture-of-Experts folders, and a linter caps each card at 1,200 tokens to limit memorization. Training uses 20 novels with three epochs and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Evaluation holds out six novels (385 episodes) and compares four configurations: Base (empty library), +Few-shot, +Distill, and +Ours. The paper reports ten event-based metrics designed with professionals, and the abstract states that generation quality improves on unseen stories. The main limitations are that the training corpus is proprietary and that the evaluation is limited to short-drama screenwriting.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Fine-tuning large language models is costly and opaque, and hand-written skills are a bottleneck, motivating self-supervised skill acquisition.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior skill methods need costly human writing or successful trajectories, so the authors summarize and reconstruct high-quality examples instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: A corruption-and-reconstruction loop trains a skill library, with capacity limits and micro-step updates to keep it organized.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Held-out evaluation compares four configurations across 385 episodes from six unseen stories using ten metrics.

repos.title: Raven: The Harness of Harnesses for Composable Agentic Intelligence
repos.paper_summary: Raven is an open-source multi-agent ecosystem that automatically constructs and orchestrates modular agent harnesses for long-horizon, cross-domain tasks. The Host Agent decomposes goals into subtasks, assigns them to specialized agents, and coordinates execution via a directed acyclic graph with explicit artifact dependencies. A diagnosis-driven evolution loop improves harness configurations by testing candidates against frozen task models, while Skill Forge retrieves reusable procedures from past executions. The paper establishes sufficient conditions under which composing multiple agents expands reliable task coverage beyond individual capabilities within a shared resource budget. On the new Multi-Agent Orchestration Benchmark (MAOB), Raven outperforms all baselines on four planning metrics using two backbone models, achieving Exact Match gains of 10.4 and 10.5 percentage points over the strongest competitor. Domain-specific evaluations show that native specialists perform competitively in research, coding, design, and operations. Experiments indicate that the curated skill library improves performance on three benchmarks, yielding larger gains than OpenClaw on two of them. The theoretical guarantees require specific compatibility conditions that may be difficult to verify for arbitrary third-party agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Raven composes model–harness agents through a host that plans, dispatches, and integrates work across domains.

digest_headlines.heading: Theory
digest_headlines.headline: Under a shared budget, sufficient conditions let composed agents reliably cover tasks that individual agents cannot reliably solve alone.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Agent Collaboration
digest_headlines.headline: A typed dependency graph is validated before dispatch, and every handoff passes through a recorded artifact.

digest_headlines.heading: Agent Harness Self-Evolution
digest_headlines.headline: Harness evolution edits a frozen model's strategy interfaces and keeps candidates only after paired screening.

digest_headlines.heading: Memory System
digest_headlines.headline: EverOS memory consolidates episodes into scenes and profiles, and Raven recalls them through hybrid retrieval.

digest_headlines.heading: Skill Forge
digest_headlines.headline: Skill Forge fuses skills from three sources, selects them through a gate, and revises skills from execution cases.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Raven ranks first on all four graph metrics under both backbones, with Exact Match gains of 10.4 and 10.5 percentage points.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans orchestration, harness evolution, agent memory, and skills, which Raven combines with explicit boundaries.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Raven's conclusion summarizes planning and skill results and proposes a multi-device network as future work.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix contains notation, execution semantics, the finite-query limit, and details of benchmark, grading, and ablation protocols.

repos.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
repos.paper_summary: This technical report evaluates GPT-6-Astra, a model whose weights stay fixed, on 12 embodied benchmarks covering tabletop manipulation, dexterous hands, humanoids, household tasks, and navigation. Under a unified protocol, the model gets a frozen knowledge package built from each benchmark's training demonstrations, and episodes run with either the standard step limit or up to 10× that limit. At the standard budget, it matches or exceeds the best published result on most settings, with the largest margins on LIBERO-Ultra-Long and DexJoCo. Reported success rates are 81.9% on RoboDojo and 87.3% on DexJoCo. On SIMPLE, task-level ICL raises success on four common tasks from 70.8% to 90.8%. In a RoboDojo harness ablation pairing the model with a π0.5 controller, closed-loop review plus ICL reaches 54.17% success, versus 15.56% for the baseline. Limitations include weaker transfer when test tasks differ from the training data, high token and time cost, and failures in physical verification, irreversible errors, and long-horizon progress.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: The report asks what a general model's embodied competence implies, and where the field should go next.

digest_headlines.heading: Large-Scale Study under A Unified Protocol
digest_headlines.headline: At the standard budget, the model matches or exceeds the best published result on most of twelve settings.

digest_headlines.heading: Harness Ablation
digest_headlines.headline: Closed-loop review improves success by up to 20.00 percentage points over open-loop execution, at higher token cost.

digest_headlines.heading: Real-World Validation
digest_headlines.headline: Zero-shot control succeeded in 17/18 rigid pick-and-place trials but 0/11 plug insertion trials.

digest_headlines.heading: Towards a Next-Generation Embodied Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: Current benchmarks were designed for imitation-trained policies, so the report proposes three principles for next-generation designs.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: GPT-6-Astra is a clear advance in embodied capability, but benchmark success does not yet imply reliable deployment.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists contributors, related work, empirical studies of frontier models, and per-platform real-world results.

repos.title: Prime Agent: A Self-Improving RLM Harness
repos.paper_summary:
Prime Agent is an open-source harness for long-horizon evaluation and coding-agent workflows. It provides a persistent IPython REPL, recursive subagents with direct agent-to-agent communication, and Continual Harness for storing versioned prompts, memories, skills, and subagent specifications across trajectories. The model controls strategy construction while the runtime standardizes execution, recovery, and resource accounting.

The paper evaluates Prime Agent against native and alternative harnesses (Pi, Claude Code, Codex) on interactive reasoning, long-context tasks, and autonomous systems construction. On ARC-AGI-3, Prime Agent raises RHAE Best@1 from 30% to 95.5%. In long-context benchmarks, it matches or exceeds baselines; for example, on OOLONG (Yahoo, 128k), GPT-5.6 Sol scores .940 with Prime Agent versus .900 with Codex. For GPU kernel generation on PMPP-Hard, Prime Agent achieves comparable solve rates at substantially reduced token cost. A seven-day Factorio run completed 24 of 196 technologies using 23.4 million output tokens. Limitations include models' poor handling of irreversible actions and online refinement potentially preserving specification exploits as reusable skills.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent argues the harness should expose expressive primitives, so evaluation measures model capability rather than harness failures.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Prime Agent Architecture
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent splits information management from computation management across persistent sessions, a daemon and Continual Harness state.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Prime Agent is generally competitive on long-context tasks and close to native harnesses on GPU-kernel generation.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work spans programmatic inference, coding-agent runtimes, ARC-AGI-3 systems and multi-agent communication, which Prime Agent combines.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Many harness capabilities remain underused because current models were not trained to operate them.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists three out-of-loop nanoGPT experiments, from Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4 Pro and a third model, plus an orchestration example.
